content: 1. A simulation study was conducted and published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2017, focusing on aircraft disinsection procedures for flights entering Australia and New Zealand. The study emphasized the use of 2% permethrin aerosol applied after aircraft servicing and before passenger boarding, with air-conditioning turned off and only one cabin door open. 2. Specific application methods and quantities of insecticide have been developed for all aircraft types, and personnel are trained to ensure proper application. The pre-embarkation aerosol spray method offers several advantages over other aerosol methods: it does not inconvenience passengers, is simple to apply by ground staff or airline crew, requires only one treatment instead of a two-stage process, saves costs and insecticide, and is easily observable by both aircraft staff and departure authorities. 3. Airlines are given the choice between residual treatment and pre-embarkation aerosol spraying. Residual treatment is more expensive but lasts for eight weeks, whereas aerosol spraying is effective for only one flight sector. The choice often depends on cost or product availability. 4. The New Zealand Ministry of Primary Industries regularly conducts bioassays using laboratory-bred houseflies on arriving aircraft to ensure compliance with residual and pre-embarkation treatments. This bioassay process was developed by the same entomologists who designed the pre-embarkation method. 5. It was suggested that the World Health Organization (WHO) update its disinsection guidelines, which have not changed since 1995, to recommend the Australia/New Zealand pre-embarkation method when passengers are not on board. However, participants were advised not to favor one technique over others, as different methods may suit different regions and situations. 6. Concerns were raised about the adequacy of the pesticide amounts recommended by WHO, as they might be too low. Additionally, aerosol spraying in the cabin up to one hour before passenger boarding may not effectively kill mosquitoes entering with passengers. Small droplets may remain airborne but can be removed once the ventilation system is activated. 7. Residual spraying in cargo holds involves treating the floor, walls, and ceiling surfaces or using aerosol sprays to knock down flying insects. Both methods leave minimal but effective residue to kill invertebrates settling on surfaces, but neither affects insects inside luggage or cargo containers. 8. Treatment of aerobridges targets mosquitoes in the cabin, while treating baggage tunnels and cargo handling areas addresses mosquitoes emerging from the aircraft hold and unit load devices. The latter is arguably more important. 9. Airlines landing in Australia with compliance agreements have options for disinsection methods, while those without agreements must use pre-flight/top-of-descent or on-arrival methods, both involving spraying with passengers on board. 10. The European Union (EU) biocidal regulations reference WHO efficacy guidelines, which require testing on aircraft with mosquito species not available in some regions. This has made permethrin testing prohibitively expensive, leading some companies to cease its supply. 11. WHO was urged to update its guidelines urgently and identify an effective replacement for permethrin. The pre-embarkation method has not elicited complaints from cabin crew, although residual spraying has caused issues when ground crew sprayed crew rest areas. 12. Aerosols are not permitted in aircraft cabins in the USA, but non-chemical disinsection methods are being tested for military use. WHO advises that currently recommended products pose no health risks when used according to label instructions. 13. The aircraft disinsection market is small and not commercially profitable, which limits the development of new products. Overuse of permethrin in agriculture has led to mosquito resistance, and pyrethroids have been widely distributed for malaria control. 14. UUDS, a French pest control company, has developed various vector control products, including residual treatments and preventive measures. Their tests revealed that catering trolleys attract cockroaches and mosquitoes, necessitating their treatment alongside the aircraft. 15. The EU's restrictions on permethrin stem from concerns about its widespread use in agriculture and potential environmental impacts, such as harm to bee populations. However, aircraft disinsection is a distinct application. 16. Cleaning frequency may affect the concentration of remaining insecticide residues. Residual spraying should be limited to cargo holds and not applied in passenger cabins or crew work areas. 17. Italy has introduced a regulation requiring residual treatment for all aircraft entering the country. This poses challenges for airlines like Lufthansa, which would need to treat hundreds of aircraft every few months. 18. Concerns were raised about the potential health risks to cabin crew from repeated exposure to permethrin. Consequently, pre-embarkation spraying is preferred by some airlines. 19. PSA-Paris has developed a product using trans-phenothrin. EU regulations require producers to justify the continued use of permethrin, and different countries impose varying restrictions on chemical substances. 20. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is working with WHO to review disinsection recommendations and explore non-chemical methods. ICAO is also considering a risk assessment model for aircraft disinsection based on vector presence and seasonal variations. 21. Non-chemical disinsection methods under investigation include air curtains, ultraviolet scanning, sonic devices, and insect repellents. WHO was asked to establish standards and performance criteria for non-chemical methods, aiming for 90% vector control. 22. The group appreciated the proposed risk model but acknowledged the difficulty of keeping it updated. Climate changes will influence the future risk of disease vectors. 23. E-mist Innovations Inc. has developed an electrostatic method for rapid insecticide application, including a hand-held device for cabin disinfection and a backpack for cargo holds. While the equipment cost may be higher, the application cost is significantly lower than chemical methods.
